sources.title: Parenting Strategies for a Child Who is Easily Frustrated
sources.publisher: ZERO TO THREE (page dated 22 Feb 2010)
sources.quote: When your child falls apart, let her know that you appreciate how hard it can be. ... Then become her coach—help your child think through solutions without doing the work for her. ... Suggest or demonstrate strategies for solving whatever problem she is facing. ... Break the challenge into manageable parts. ... Offer time away from the frustrating task for a hug or a cozy snuggle with a book. ... Then return to the challenge with new energy.
sources.supports: Acknowledge how hard it is, coach instead of doing it for the child, suggest or show a strategy, break the challenge into parts, offer a break with a hug and return with new energy.

sources.title: How to Help Kids Learn to Fail
sources.publisher: Child Mind Institute (last reviewed or updated 6 May 2025)
sources.quote: When your kid does fail at something, let them know you see how frustrated and disappointed they are. ... Skipping right to bouncing back doesn't give kids the time they need to feel their feelings. ... When your kid is ready, talk about what went wrong and how they might do things differently next time. ... You and your child can try to come up with what they could do the next time for a better chance at success.
sources.supports: Name the frustration first, give time to feel it, and when the child is ready talk about what to do differently next time.

sources.title: How to Support Young Kids Who Are Struggling in School
sources.publisher: Child Mind Institute (last reviewed or updated 7 Nov 2025, Rae Jacobson)
sources.quote: Help kids build their resilience by doing small bursts of difficult work ... Praising your child’s efforts instead of focusing on results will help them feel more comfortable trying things ... Managing frustration without blowing up, or giving up, is an essential skill for kids (and grownups)
sources.supports: Short bursts of difficult work build resilience, and praising effort rather than results makes trying feel safer. The page is about school; applied here to any hard task at home.

sources.title: Recommended Reading: Books to Teach Kids About Feelings & Resilience
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 24 Apr 2025)
sources.quote: Reading books together about common feelings can help children recognize their own emotions. It can also help them develop empathy, understanding how others may be feeling.
sources.supports: Reading together about feelings helps children recognise their own and understand others'. Used only as support for reading stories about a hard moment; no promise of a result.

sources.publisher: ZERO TO THREE (page dated 22 Feb 2010)
sources.quote: When your child falls apart, let her know that you appreciate how hard it can be. ... Then become her coach—help your child think through solutions without doing the work for her. ... Suggest or demonstrate strategies for solving whatever problem she is facing. ... Break the challenge into manageable parts. ... Offer time away from the frustrating task for a hug or a cozy snuggle with a book. ... Then return to the challenge with new energy.
sources.supports: Acknowledge how hard it is, coach instead of doing it for the child, suggest or show a strategy, break the challenge into parts, offer a break with a hug and return with new energy.

sources.title: How to Help Kids Learn to Fail
sources.publisher: Child Mind Institute (last reviewed or updated 6 May 2025)
sources.quote: When your kid does fail at something, let them know you see how frustrated and disappointed they are. ... Skipping right to bouncing back doesn't give kids the time they need to feel their feelings. ... When your kid is ready, talk about what went wrong and how they might do things differently next time. ... You and your child can try to come up with what they could do the next time for a better chance at success.
sources.supports: Name the frustration first, give time to feel it, and when the child is ready talk about what to do differently next time.

sources.publisher: Child Mind Institute (last reviewed or updated 7 Nov 2025, Rae Jacobson)

sources.quote: Help your child see the situation from the other child's point of view ... Once they understand what they've done wrong—but not before—ask them to apologize to the other child. ... simply saying "I'm sorry" may not help your child correct their behavior ... they also need to know why they're apologizing ... They may not understand right away, but give it time. ... Let them know you understand and accept their feelings.
sources.supports: Help the child see the other child's side, ask for an apology only once they understand, explain why they apologize, give it time, and accept their feelings.

sources.title: Communication Skills Start at Home
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 16 Mar 2023)
sources.quote: We often teach children to say "I'm sorry" without teaching them to acknowledge the issue. ... I am sorry I yelled at you. Mommy felt frustrated with the mess. ... Model full apologies ("I am sorry for..."). ... Focus on the behavior, not the child.
sources.supports: Teach the child to name what happened, model a full apology that says what you are sorry for, and talk about the behavior, not the child.
